questions.stem: For approximately how long has life existed on Earth?
options: About 350 million years
About 35 million years
About 13.8 billion years
About 3.5 billion years
questions.explanation: The oldest evidence of life, including fossil stromatolites from the Pilbara in Western Australia, is about 3.5 billion years old. About 13.8 billion years is the age of the universe, not of life on Earth.

questions.stem: Why is a comparison of DNA sequences (comparative genomics) strong evidence for evolution?
options: Species sharing a recent common ancestor have more similar sequences
Every species has an identical DNA sequence for each one of its genes
DNA sequences change only when a species moves into a new habitat
Closely related species always have the same number of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Mutations build up in DNA over time, so species that diverged recently have had less time to accumulate differences. Sequences are not identical between species, and chromosome number can differ even between close relatives.

questions.stem: A protein found in many organisms is sequenced. Number of amino acid differences from the human sequence: monkey 1, dog 11, snake 14, yeast 45. What do these data best support?
options: Humans evolved from monkeys, which differ by only one amino acid
Yeast is the most recently evolved species, as it has the most changes
Dogs and snakes are each other's closest relatives in this list
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with dogs than with snakes
questions.explanation: Fewer amino acid differences indicate a more recent common ancestor, so humans are more closely related to dogs (11) than to snakes (14). Shared ancestry does not mean humans descended from living monkeys, and these data compare each species only with humans.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of humans, whales, bats and cats have the same arrangement of bones but different functions. What are these structures called?
options: Vestigial structures
Transitional structures
Homologous structures
Analogous structures
questions.explanation: Homologous structures share an underlying plan inherited from a common ancestor, even though they are now used differently. Analogous structures do a similar job but evolved separately.

questions.stem: The wings of birds and the wings of insects both allow flight, but are built in completely different ways. What do they show?
options: Convergent evolution of analogous structures in unrelated groups
Divergent evolution of homologous structures from a shared ancestor
Descent from a recent common ancestor that also had wings
Vestigial structures left over from an earlier way of life
questions.explanation: Analogous structures arise when similar selection pressures act on unrelated groups, so they look alike in function but not in structure. They are not evidence of a recent common ancestor.

questions.stem: Early embryos of fish, birds and humans all have pharyngeal arches and a tail. What does this suggest?
options: These vertebrates inherited developmental genes from a common ancestor
Humans pass through a fish stage and a bird stage before being born
The embryos have identical DNA right up until the later stages of development
The features formed separately because each embryo develops in water
questions.explanation: Similar early stages of development reflect shared developmental genes inherited from a common ancestor. Embryos do not repeat the adult forms of other groups, and their DNA differs from the start.

questions.stem: What makes a fossil such as Archaeopteryx, with feathers and wings as well as teeth and a bony tail, useful evidence for evolution?
options: It is the oldest fossil ever found, so it marks the start of all life
It is a transitional form showing features of two different groups
It proves that every modern bird evolved from that one individual
It shows that reptiles and birds have always lived as separate groups
questions.explanation: Transitional fossils combine features of an ancestral group and a descendant group, here reptiles and birds, supporting change over time. One fossil cannot prove direct descent of all birds from that particular animal.

questions.stem: In undisturbed sedimentary rock, simple single-celled fossils occur in the lowest layers and increasingly complex organisms appear in higher layers. What does this pattern support?
options: All organisms appeared at the same time and later sorted by their weight
Complex organisms evolved first and later simplified into single cells
Fossils form only in the upper layers, so the lower layers hold no complex life
Life has changed and diversified over time, with older forms in deeper layers
questions.explanation: In undisturbed rock, deeper layers are older, so the fossil record shows a sequence from simple early life to more complex and diverse later forms. This is consistent with gradual change and diversification over billions of years.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, what is represented by the point where two branches split?
options: The most recent common ancestor of the groups that branch from it
A living species that is the direct parent of all branches above it
An extinction event that removed the species on one branch
The point where two separate species hybridised to form one
questions.explanation: Each branching point represents a common ancestor, from which the descendant lineages diverged. Living species sit at the tips, not at the nodes.

questions.stem: In a phylogenetic tree, species P and Q share a node, and that branch joins species R at an older node. Species S branches off at the oldest node. Which statement is correct?
options: P and Q evolved from R, which is their parent
P is more closely related to R than it is to S
R is more closely related to S than it is to Q
S is the ancestor of P, Q and R in the tree
questions.explanation: P shares a more recent common ancestor with R (the second node) than with S (the oldest node), so P and R are closer relatives. Living species at the tips are not ancestors of one another.

questions.stem: Which kinds of information can be used to construct a phylogenetic tree?
options: Protein sequences, DNA sequences and anatomical features
Only the external colour and size of each species
Only where each species lives and what it eats today
Only the dates when each species was first named
questions.explanation: Trees are built from shared characteristics that reflect relatedness, such as genomic, protein and anatomical data, often combined. Habitat, diet or colour alone can reflect convergent evolution rather than common ancestry.

questions.stem: Mutation is often called the ultimate source of genetic variation. Why?
options: It is the only process that creates new alleles
It is the only process that changes allele frequencies
It always produces alleles that improve survival
It shuffles existing alleles into new combinations
questions.explanation: New alleles arise only through mutation; other processes such as selection, drift and gene flow change the frequencies of alleles that already exist. Shuffling existing alleles is what meiosis and fertilisation do.

questions.stem: What is a selection pressure?
options: The effort an individual makes to change its own traits during its lifetime
An environmental factor that affects which phenotypes survive and reproduce
A force inside an organism that causes it to mutate when it is in need
The pressure on a population to move to a new and better environment
questions.explanation: Selection pressures such as predators, disease, climate or food supply give some phenotypes a survival and reproductive advantage. They do not cause the mutations that produce new variation.

questions.stem: After an antibiotic is used heavily in a hospital, most of the Staphylococcus bacteria there are resistant to it. Which explanation is correct?
options: The antibiotic made the bacteria mutate until every cell became resistant to it
Resistant bacteria already present survived and reproduced, so their allele increased
The antibiotic caused the bacteria to develop resistance so that they could all survive
Bacteria learned to resist the antibiotic and passed on what they had learned
questions.explanation: Resistance alleles arose by chance mutation before the antibiotic was used; the antibiotic killed susceptible cells, leaving resistant ones to multiply. The selection pressure acts on existing variation and does not direct which mutations occur.

questions.stem: Cane toads at the advancing front of their spread across northern Australia have longer legs, on average, than toads in long-established populations. Which explanation fits natural selection?
options: Toads at the front need longer legs, so their genes change to produce them
Longer-legged toads move further, so they reach the front and breed with each other
Toads at the front stretch their legs by hopping more and pass longer legs on
New habitats cause mutations for longer legs in toads that arrive there first
questions.explanation: Toads with longer legs disperse faster, so they are over-represented at the front, where they mate with each other, raising the frequency of alleles for long legs there. Characteristics acquired by use are not inherited.

questions.stem: In natural selection, what does it mean for a phenotype to have a selective advantage?
options: Individuals with it live longer, whether or not they reproduce
Individuals with it are always the largest and strongest
Individuals with it can choose to change their own genes
Individuals with it are more likely to survive and leave offspring
questions.explanation: Selective advantage is measured by survival and reproduction, so the alleles behind the phenotype are passed on more often. Living longer without reproducing does not change allele frequencies.

questions.stem: When myxoma virus was released in Australia it killed most wild rabbits, but within years rabbit populations recovered and far fewer rabbits died from infection. What best explains the recovery?
options: The rabbits learned to avoid infected rabbits and taught this to their young
Rabbits with alleles for resistance survived and bred, raising the allele's frequency
Surviving rabbits developed resistance during infection and passed it to offspring
The virus caused rabbits to mutate so that every survivor became fully resistant
questions.explanation: Some rabbits carried alleles giving partial resistance, and the virus selected for them, so resistance became more common in the population. The virus also evolved to become less lethal, but changes acquired during a rabbit's life are not inherited.

questions.stem: Which definition of a gene pool is correct?
options: All the alleles of all the genes in a population
All the genes found together on a single chromosome
The pair of alleles one individual carries
The set of genes shared by every species
questions.explanation: A gene pool is the total set of alleles present in an interbreeding population at a given time. The alleles one individual carries are its genotype.

questions.stem: In a population of 200 beetles, 60 are BB, 100 are Bb and 40 are bb. What is the frequency of the b allele?
questions.explanation: There are 400 alleles in total. The b alleles number 100 (from Bb) + 80 (from bb) = 180, and 180 / 400 = 0.45. Using only the bb count (40/200 = 0.20) gives the genotype frequency, not the allele frequency.

questions.stem: Which statement about random genetic drift is correct?
options: It changes allele frequencies by chance and has most effect in small populations
It changes allele frequencies to suit the environment, mainly in large populations
It produces new alleles by mutation each time a population becomes smaller
It always increases genetic diversity by adding alleles from other populations
questions.explanation: Drift is random change in allele frequency from one generation to the next, and in a small population chance events can quickly fix or remove an allele. Adding alleles from other populations is gene flow.

questions.stem: A storm carries a few lizards to an uninhabited island, where they found a new population. An allele that is rare on the mainland is common on the island. What is this an example of?
options: The founder effect
Gene flow
Natural selection
Selective breeding
questions.explanation: The founder effect is a type of genetic drift: a few founders carry only a chance sample of the source population's alleles. Natural selection would require the allele to give an advantage on the island.

questions.stem: Which observation would best indicate that genetic drift, rather than natural selection, caused a change in allele frequency in a small population?
options: The population is large and individuals breed with migrants
The change happened in step with a new predator arriving
The allele that increased gives no advantage in that environment
The allele that increased clearly improves survival in that habitat
questions.explanation: Drift changes frequencies by chance, regardless of whether alleles are beneficial, so a rise in a neutral allele points to drift. A change linked to survival or a new predator points to selection.

questions.stem: Two neighbouring populations of a frog species are joined when a drain is built between their ponds, and frogs move between them. What is the most likely effect?
options: Gene flow makes the allele frequencies of the populations more alike
Gene flow makes the allele frequencies of the populations less alike
Each population becomes a separate species within a generation
Genetic drift increases because the populations become smaller
questions.explanation: Migration carries alleles between populations, which tends to even out their allele frequencies. Reduced gene flow, not increased, allows populations to diverge.

questions.stem: Which list gives four processes that change allele frequencies in a gene pool?
options: Mitosis, natural selection, transcription and gene flow
Mutation, translation, genetic drift and photosynthesis
Binary fission, osmosis, genetic drift and gene flow
Mutation, natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow
questions.explanation: Gene pools are dynamic, with allele frequencies changed by mutation, differing selection pressures, random genetic drift and changes in gene flow. Transcription and translation express genes but do not change allele frequencies.

questions.stem: How are micro-evolution and macro-evolution related?
options: Micro-evolution happens only in plants and macro-evolution in animals
Micro-evolution reverses macro-evolution, so species return to old forms
Speciation results from many small allele frequency changes over time
Macro-evolution happens suddenly and does not involve allele changes
questions.explanation: Micro-evolution is change in allele frequencies within a population; accumulated over many generations it produces new species and larger groups. The two are the same process viewed over different time scales.

questions.stem: What is selective breeding (artificial selection)?
options: Individuals with useful traits surviving better out in the wild
Inserting a gene from one species into another species
Chance changes in the alleles of a small population
Humans choosing which individuals with desired traits reproduce
questions.explanation: In selective breeding people choose parents with desirable characteristics, so allele frequencies in the domestic gene pool change over generations. Survival in the wild without human choice is natural selection.

questions.stem: Many generations of selecting merino sheep for fine wool have produced flocks with very similar fleeces. What has most likely happened to the gene pool of these flocks?
options: Alleles for fine wool rose in frequency and overall genetic diversity fell
New alleles for fine wool were created by the breeders' selection choices
Every allele in the flock became equally common through many generations
Genetic diversity rose because breeders chose the most varied animals
questions.explanation: Breeding only from animals with desired traits raises the frequency of the alleles behind them and removes others, reducing diversity. Selection acts on existing alleles; it does not create new ones.

questions.stem: What is required for allopatric speciation to begin?
options: Hybridisation between two different existing species
A large population with constant gene flow throughout
Identical selection pressures across the species' range
Geographic isolation of populations of one species
questions.explanation: Allopatric speciation starts when a physical barrier such as a mountain range, river or sea splits a population. Gene flow stops, and the separated populations can then diverge.

questions.stem: Why do geographically isolated populations of one species tend to diverge over time?
options: Gene flow between them speeds up, so they quickly exchange their differences
Both face identical environments, so the same alleles become fixed in each
Different selection pressures, mutations and drift act on each, with no gene flow
Each population mutates in response to its needs until the two look different
questions.explanation: Without gene flow, each population's gene pool changes independently through its own mutations, drift and selection pressures. Over time the differences can become large enough to prevent interbreeding.

questions.stem: Two populations of a bird species were separated for a long time. When brought together, they mate but produce no fertile offspring. What does this indicate?
options: Gene flow between them has increased since they were reunited
The founder effect has made the two populations genetically identical
Reproductive isolation has developed, so they are now separate species
They are still one species, because they will still attempt to mate
questions.explanation: Producing no fertile offspring shows the populations are reproductively isolated, completing allopatric speciation. Willingness to mate does not make them one species if no fertile offspring result.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of events in allopatric speciation?
options: Different selection pressures, then gene flow, then geographic isolation
Hybridisation, then geographic isolation, then a single shared gene pool
Isolation, then different selection pressures, then reproductive isolation
Reproductive isolation, then geographic isolation, then new selection pressures
questions.explanation: A barrier first separates the populations, differing selection pressures and other processes change their gene pools, and eventually they can no longer interbreed. Reproductive isolation is the end point, not the start.

questions.stem: Why are populations with reduced genetic diversity at greater risk of extinction?
options: Their members cannot reproduce sexually, so no offspring vary at all
Fewer individuals may carry alleles that help them survive a new threat
They have more alleles in total, so harmful ones are more likely to be expressed
They grow faster than diverse populations and soon run out of food
questions.explanation: With little variation, a new disease, predator or climate change may affect every individual in the same way, leaving none able to survive. Inbreeding in small populations also raises the chance of harmful recessive conditions.

questions.stem: A population of an endangered wallaby falls to 30 animals and later recovers to 2000. Compared with before the decline, what is the recovered population most likely to have?
options: The same genetic diversity, because each survivor carried every allele
No genetic diversity, because every animal is now a clone of one survivor
Less genetic diversity, because many alleles were lost when numbers fell
More genetic diversity, because the population has grown so much larger
questions.explanation: When a population falls sharply, the survivors carry only a fraction of the original alleles, and drift removes more while numbers are low. Regrowth restores numbers but not the lost alleles, which can only return by mutation or gene flow.

questions.stem: Conservation managers move a few individuals of a threatened possum between two small, isolated populations. What is the main genetic benefit?
options: Gene flow adds alleles, increasing diversity and reducing inbreeding
Moving animals causes useful mutations to arise in each population
It keeps the two populations separate so that each becomes a new species
It removes all harmful recessive alleles from both populations at once
questions.explanation: Translocating animals restores gene flow, bringing new alleles into each small population and lowering the risk of inbreeding. It does not produce mutations or remove all harmful alleles.

questions.stem: Natural selection acts on phenotypes. How does this change the gene pool?
options: Selection removes all variation, so a single allele remains in every population
Alleles behind favoured phenotypes are passed on more, so their frequency rises
Each individual's alleles change during its life to match the favoured phenotype
Selection creates new alleles that produce the phenotypes the environment needs
questions.explanation: Individuals with favoured phenotypes leave more offspring, so the alleles responsible become more common in the next generation. Individuals do not change their alleles, and selection works on variation that already exists.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between species shown by comparative anatomy, embryology, proteins and genomics?
options: They show that each species was formed separately and has not changed
They show that all modern species evolved from the same living species
They show that species become more similar to one another over time
They agree in showing that species are related through common ancestors
questions.explanation: Independent lines of evidence give largely consistent patterns of relatedness, which supports the theory of evolution from common ancestors. Living species share ancestors; they did not evolve from one another.

questions.stem: A biologist finds that two species of fish look almost identical but their DNA differs greatly, while another pair look very different but have very similar DNA. Which pair is more closely related?
options: Both pairs equally, since appearance and DNA balance out
Neither, since DNA cannot show evolutionary relationships
The pair that look different but have very similar DNA
The pair that look almost identical but differ greatly in DNA
questions.explanation: DNA similarity reflects shared ancestry directly, whereas similar appearance can arise from convergent evolution in similar environments. So the pair with very similar DNA share the more recent common ancestor.
